message:
QUESTION:
How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?

DATA:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.

<analysis>
# Average-speed cameras: three-year evaluation

## Summary

- **Raw fall.** Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites fell by 35%, from 156 in 2020–22 to 102 in 2023–25.
- **Not all of that fall is due to the cameras.**
  - Collisions fell by 10% on other city roads over the same period.
  - Traffic through the sites fell by 15%, mainly because a new bypass opened two months after the cameras were installed.
  - The sites were chosen because their collision counts were the highest in the city, so some fall was likely anyway (regression to the mean).
- **Best estimate.** After allowing for the city-wide trend and the traffic fall, the cameras reduced injury collisions by **about 15%**, or roughly 6 collisions a year across the 10 sites.
  - This is an uncertain central estimate, not a ceiling. Regression to the mean would make the true effect smaller. Our traffic adjustment is probably too large, which would make the true effect bigger. We cannot tell which bias is larger.
  - The statistical uncertainty is wide, from about a 34% reduction to a 10% increase. A zero effect cannot be ruled out on collision counts alone.
- **Speed evidence.** Mean speeds fell from 34 to 31 mph even though lighter traffic would tend to raise speeds. This is the clearest sign that the cameras changed driver behaviour. On standard speed–collision relationships it is consistent with a reduction of about 15–17%.
- **City-wide rollout.** **We cannot estimate what a city-wide rollout would achieve.** The cameras were tested only on high-collision arterial roads, which make up 1.3% of the network. Most of the network is residential streets that differ greatly from these sites. The only defensible statement covers similar arterial roads (see below).
- **Recommendation.** Do not fund a city-wide programme on this evidence. Compare the 4 sites unaffected by the bypass with the 6 that were affected. Then consider a staged, properly evaluated extension to similar arterial roads.

## Background

- **Installation.** Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023.
- **Coverage.** All 10 sites are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, about 1.3% of its length.
- **Site selection.** The sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020–22.
- **Comparison.** This note compares injury collisions in the three years before installation (2020–22) with the three years after (2023–25), at the 10 sites and on all other city roads.

## Results, step by step

| | Sites: collisions/yr | Change | Effect attributed to cameras |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before (2020–22) | 52.0 | | |
| After (2023–25), observed | 34.0 | −35% | |
| Expected after, allowing for the city-wide trend (×0.90) | 46.8 | | ~27% (≈13/yr) |
| Expected after, also allowing for the 15% traffic fall (×0.85) | 39.8 | | **~15% (≈6/yr)** |
| Remaining biases (see steps 2 and 3) | not estimable from these data | | could be higher or lower than 15% |

**1. Background trend.** Collisions on other roads fell from 1,200 to 1,080 a year, a 10% fall. Relative to that trend, the reduction at the sites is about 27% (0.654 / 0.900 = 0.727).

The comparison period includes 2020–21, when COVID restrictions disrupted traffic across the city. Comparing with other roads accounts for much of this. However, arterial roads and residential streets may have been affected differently, so some distortion may remain.

**2. Traffic.** The bypass opened in March 2023, two months after the cameras. It diverted through-traffic from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic at the sites fell by an average of 15%, while traffic elsewhere was broadly unchanged. Fewer vehicles means fewer collisions, whatever the cameras do.

- **Proportional adjustment.** If collisions fell in proportion to traffic, we would expect 52 × 0.90 × 0.85 ≈ 39.8 collisions a year without cameras, against 34 observed. That gives a camera effect of about 15%.
- **Why this adjustment is probably too large.** Collisions usually rise and fall *less* than proportionally with traffic. If a 15% traffic fall reduced collisions by only 8–11%, the camera effect would be roughly 18–21%. The 15% figure may therefore understate the effect. Against this, lighter traffic can raise speeds, which would push collisions up somewhat.
- **The effect is concentrated.** A 15% average fall driven by 6 of the 10 sites implies traffic fell by roughly 25% at those 6 and changed little at the other 4. The 4 unaffected sites therefore give the cleanest available test of the cameras alone. Site-level collision data should be obtained before any decision (Recommendation 1).

**3. Regression to the mean.** The sites were chosen *because* they had the highest collision counts in 2020–22.

- Sites selected on an unusually high count tend to record fewer collisions in the next period anyway, partly through chance.
- So 2020–22 overstates what these sites would normally experience, and the 15% figure includes some fall that would have happened anyway.
- With only one before-period, we cannot estimate the size of this bias. At hotspot camera schemes it is often substantial. Here, the speed evidence (below) suggests it may be modest.

**Net effect of steps 2 and 3.** Regression to the mean pushes the true effect below 15%. The traffic adjustment probably pushes it above 15%. We treat 15% as a central estimate. The true effect could plausibly lie anywhere from about 10% to about 20%, and statistical noise widens that range further.

**4. Statistical uncertainty.** The counts at the sites are small.

- The approximate 95% interval on the raw before/after ratio is 0.51–0.84.
- After the trend and traffic adjustments, the interval on the camera effect runs from about a **34% reduction to a 10% increase**.
- This interval treats the 15% traffic fall as exactly known. It is itself an average estimate, so the true interval is somewhat wider.
- On collision counts alone, therefore, a zero effect cannot be ruled out.

## Speeds

- **Figures.** Mean speeds at the camera sites fell from 34 mph to 31 mph. Typical speeds are now close to the 30 mph limit, though still slightly above it.
- **Why this matters.** This is the strongest evidence that the cameras work.
  - The fall happened even though traffic got lighter. Lighter traffic would tend to *raise* free-flow speeds, so the bypass cannot plausibly explain the fall.
  - Regression to the mean in collision counts does not affect speeds in the same way.
- **What it implies for collisions.** Under the widely used "power model", injury collisions vary roughly with the square of mean speed. On that basis, (31/34)² ≈ 0.83 predicts about a 17% fall in injury collisions. This agrees well with the adjusted estimate of about 15%. It suggests the true effect is not far below 15%, and that the regression-to-the-mean bias may be smaller than is typical for hotspot schemes.
- **Limits.**
  - The power model is an average relationship, and it uses mean speed only. It says nothing about the fastest drivers, who contribute disproportionately to injury collisions.
  - The surveys do not say whether before and after conditions (time of day, weather, survey method) were comparable.
  - The speed evidence therefore supports the estimate but does not pin it down.

## What would a city-wide rollout achieve?

**We cannot estimate a city-wide effect from these data.** There are four reasons:

1. **The tested sites are not typical.** The cameras were evaluated only on high-collision arterial roads, which make up 1.3% of the network. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts and typically lower speeds. Cameras there would have far fewer collisions and much less speeding to prevent.
2. **There would be no hotspot effect elsewhere.** Part of the fall at the original sites probably reflects their unusually high starting point. Ordinary roads would not show this.
3. **Full coverage is not feasible.** Average-speed cameras need defined routes between camera points. Covering 900 km of mostly residential streets is not a realistic deployment.
4. **The effect estimate itself is uncertain.** Even at the tested sites, we cannot rule out a zero effect statistically.

**What can be said about similar arterial roads.**

- On other arterial roads with documented speeding, a reduction of around 15% of existing injury collisions is plausible, with wide uncertainty.
- The original sites averaged 5.2 injury collisions a year each before installation, so a 15% effect there is about 0.6 collisions per site a year.
- Other arterials were not among the city's top 10, so they will have fewer collisions to start with. A realistic figure is therefore **roughly 0.5 collisions per site a year or less, and highly uncertain.**
- On the residential network, we have no evidence either way.

## Recommendations

1. **Get site-level data first.** Compare collisions at the 4 sites unaffected by the bypass with the 6 that were affected. The 4 unaffected sites give the cleanest available test of the cameras. Also obtain site-level speed data.
2. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
3. **Get longer baselines.** Obtain collision data for 2015–19 at the 10 sites. This would:
   - show how far 2020–22 was an unusual peak, and
   - allow a formal regression-to-the-mean adjustment (empirical Bayes).
   It would also avoid relying on a baseline distorted by COVID-era traffic.
4. **Extend in stages, if at all.** If further installation is considered:
   - use arterial routes with documented speeding;
   - install in stages, with untreated comparison routes, so the effect can be measured rather than assumed.
5. **Build a business case.** Weigh installation, maintenance and enforcement costs against a realistic estimate of collisions prevented. Use roughly 0.5 per site a year or less, with sensitivity analysis across the 10–20% range.
6. **Monitor and publish.** Continue annual monitoring of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites. Publish the evaluation, including its limitations.

---

### Cover note (not part of the report)

Changes made in response to review:

- **The 15% figure is now a central estimate, not an upper bound.** The report explains that regression to the mean and the proportional traffic adjustment bias it in opposite directions.
- **The speed evidence is now reconciled with the collision estimate.** The 34→31 mph fall happened despite lighter traffic. The power model's ~17% prediction suggests the regression-to-the-mean bias may be modest.
- **The 6/4 site split is now explicit.** The Traffic section states it, and site-level comparison is now Recommendation 1.
- **The "0.5 collisions per site a year" figure is now derived.** It comes from 15% × 5.2/yr ≈ 0.6, adjusted down for lower-risk sites, and is flagged as highly uncertain.
- **The adjusted interval is stated as −34% to +10%.** The report notes it excludes uncertainty in the traffic figure.
- **A COVID baseline caveat has been added.**
- **The city-wide question is now answered directly** in the summary and the rollout section.
- **All references to the earlier draft have been removed from the report body.** These were the 26 mph error, the 290-collision extrapolation and the "fair baseline" claim.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review: Average-speed camera evaluation

The analysis is sound. It identifies the main confounders (background trend, the bypass, regression to the mean), declines to extrapolate city-wide, and keeps its uncertainty visible. I re-derived the core figures and they check out: 52 → 34 a year (−35%), the 27% trend-adjusted and 15% traffic-adjusted effects, the 18–21% range under less-than-proportional traffic effects, the raw interval of 0.51–0.84, and the adjusted interval of −34% to +10%.

There is one arithmetic error. Several inferences also go further than the data support.

## 1. Arithmetic error in the per-site figure

The rollout section says "a 15% effect there is about 0.6 collisions per site a year," based on 5.2 a year. The cover note repeats "15% × 5.2/yr ≈ 0.6." But **15% × 5.2 = 0.78**, not 0.6.

The 0.6 figure is actually 5.8 prevented a year ÷ 10 sites. That is 15% of the *counterfactual* of 3.98 a year per site, not of the raw before count. The "≈0.5 or less" conclusion probably still holds, but the derivation must be corrected. Either:
- use the counterfactual (15% × ~4.0 ≈ 0.6), or
- state 0.78 and then explain the downward adjustment.

Also note that the 5.2 baseline is itself inflated by regression to the mean. That is another reason to anchor on the lower figure.

## 2. The "10% to 20%" range is not supported

The report says the size of the regression-to-the-mean bias "cannot be estimated" and is "often substantial" at hotspot schemes. It then gives a plausible range of 10–20%. Nothing in the data supports the 10% lower bound. If regression to the mean is large, the true effect could be well below 10%, and the collision data alone don't exclude zero.

**Fix:** Drop the 10% floor or label it as judgement. In Recommendation 5, extend the sensitivity analysis to include 0–5%, not just 10–20%.

## 3. The speed evidence is used to say too much

**a) The bypass could plausibly lower mean speeds.** The report says lighter traffic raises speeds, so "the bypass cannot plausibly explain the fall." That ignores a change in who is driving. The bypass removed *through-traffic*, which on arterials is often the faster, longer-distance part of the flow. Taking it out could lower mean speed even as volumes fall. Site-level speeds for the 4 unaffected sites against the 6 affected ones would settle this. Add it to Recommendation 1 explicitly, not just "obtain site-level speed data."

**b) "Regression to the mean may be modest" is weak triangulation.**
- The power model's ~17% has wide uncertainty of its own. Exponents for urban injury collisions are often below 2. An exponent of 1.5 gives about 13%.
- The collision estimate it is compared with runs from −34% to +10%.
- Agreement between two estimates this loose cannot show that regression to the mean is small. At most, the two are "not inconsistent."

Soften the speed section and the cover note accordingly. This also removes a tension with the summary, which says "we cannot tell which bias is larger."

**c) Minor inconsistency.** The summary says the speed evidence implies "about 15–17%," but the body computes 17% only. Either show the range of exponents behind the 15% or say 17% in both places.

## 4. Where did the diverted traffic go?

The report adjusts for the 15% traffic fall but doesn't ask where those vehicles went.
- **The bypass.** If the bypass counts as a "city road," its new collisions sit in the comparison group. That makes the background trend look weaker than it is and overstates the camera effect. If it is excluded, collisions that moved onto it are simply uncounted. Either way, state which it is.
- **Diversion caused by the cameras.** Some drivers may avoid the camera routes. Collisions displaced to other roads are not prevented, and some of the traffic fall may be caused by the cameras rather than the bypass. This is worth one sentence.

## 5. Statistical interval

The −34% to +10% interval assumes Poisson variation. Collision counts are usually overdispersed, so the true interval is wider still. The report already notes that it ignores uncertainty in the traffic figure. Add overdispersion as a second reason.

## 6. Smaller points

- **COVID direction.** Restrictions in 2020–21 probably *lowered* baseline collisions. That partly offsets regression to the mean rather than adding to it. One clause saying the direction is ambiguous would help.
- **Limits of the 4-vs-6 comparison.** The 4 unaffected sites have only about 20 collisions a year between them, so this comparison will be very noisy. Recommendation 1 should set that expectation, so a null or extreme result isn't over-read. The longer 2015–19 baseline (Recommendation 3) is arguably more valuable.
- **The "~25% at the 6 sites" figure.** This is an inference that assumes the other 4 sites were unchanged. Say "if traffic at the other 4 was roughly unchanged…" rather than "implies."

## Verdict

The analysis answers the question well. The cameras probably reduced injury collisions somewhat, with a central estimate near 15% but a zero effect not excluded, and a city-wide figure cannot be estimated. Before it is circulated:
- correct the 0.6 derivation,
- remove or qualify the 10% floor,
- tone down the claims based on speed, and
- address the composition of diverted traffic and the bypass accounting.

None of these changes the recommendations. They mainly widen the stated uncertainty, which strengthens the case against a city-wide programme.
</review>

- **Is the bypass in the comparison group?** The data do not say whether the new bypass counts as an "other city road".
  - If it does, collisions on it are added to the comparison group in 2023–25. That makes the background fall look smaller than it really was, and so overstates the camera effect.
  - If it does not, collisions that moved onto the bypass with the diverted traffic are not counted anywhere.
  - This should be confirmed with the data provider. Either way, the 3,240 comparison count is large, so the effect on the estimate is probably small.

**4. Statistical uncertainty.** The counts at the sites are small.

- The approximate 95% interval on the raw before/after ratio is 0.51–0.84.

- **The bypass may have contributed.** Lighter traffic would normally *raise* speeds.   - With a power of 1.5: (31/34)^1.5 ≈ 0.87, a fall of about 13%.

- **Other limits.**

  - The surveys do not say whether before and after conditions (time of day, weather, survey method) were comparable.

**We cannot estimate a city-wide effect from these data.** There are four reasons:

1. **The tested sites are not typical.** The cameras were evaluated only on high-collision arterial roads, which make up 1.3% of the network. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts and typically lower speeds. Cameras there would have far fewer collisions and much less speeding to prevent.
2. **There would be no hotspot effect elsewhere.** Part of the fall at the original sites probably reflects their unusually high starting point. Ordinary roads would not show this.
3. **Full coverage is not feasible.** Average-speed cameras need defined routes between camera points. Covering 900 km of mostly residential streets is not a realistic deployment.
4. **The effect estimate itself is uncertain.** Even at the tested sites, we cannot rule out a zero effect.

**What can be said about similar arterial roads.**

- On other arterial roads with documented speeding, a reduction of up to about 15% of existing injury collisions is plausible. A much smaller effect, or none, cannot be excluded.
- At the original sites, the expected count without cameras was about 4.0 collisions per site a year (39.8 ÷ 10). A 15% effect is therefore about **0.6 collisions per site a year**, consistent with the ≈5.8 a year prevented across all 10. We do not use the raw before count of 5.2 a year: it is inflated by regression to the mean, and 15% of it (0.78) would overstate the benefit.
- Other arterials were not among the city's top 10, so they will have fewer collisions to start with. A realistic figure is therefore **roughly 0.5 collisions per site a year or less, possibly none, and highly uncertain.**
- On the residential network, we have no evidence either way.

## Recommendations

1. **Get a longer baseline first.** Obtain collision data for 2015–19 at the 10 sites. This is probably the most valuable single step. It would:
   - show how far 2020–22 was an unusual peak;
   - allow a formal regression-to-the-mean adjustment (empirical Bayes);
   - reduce reliance on a baseline distorted by COVID-era traffic.
2. **Get site-level data.**
   - Compare collisions at the 4 sites unaffected by the bypass with the 6 that were affected.
   - Compare **speeds** at the same two groups. This would show whether the fall in mean speed came from the cameras or from the bypass removing faster through-traffic.
   - Expect the collision comparison to be noisy. If collisions were spread roughly evenly, the 4 unaffected sites had only about 20 a year between them. A null or extreme result there should not be over-read.
3. **Clarify the comparison group.** Confirm whether the bypass is included in "other city roads". Where possible, check for collision increases on likely diversion routes around the camera sites.
4. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
5. **Extend in stages, if at all.** If further installation is considered:
   - use arterial routes with documented speeding;
   - install in stages, with untreated comparison routes, so the effect can be measured rather than assumed.
6. **Build a business case.** Weigh installation, maintenance and enforcement costs against a realistic estimate of collisions prevented. Use roughly 0.5 per site a year or less as the central figure. Test sensitivity across an effect of **0–20%**, about 0 to 0.8 collisions per site a year at sites like the originals and less elsewhere. Check whether the case survives if the effect is only 0–5%.
7. **Monitor and publish.** Continue annual monitoring of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites. Publish the evaluation, including its limitations.

---

### Cover note (not part of the report)

Changes made in response to the review:

- **Per-site figure corrected.** The 0.6 collisions per site a year is now derived as 15% of the counterfactual (≈4.0/yr per site), not of the raw 5.2/yr. The report explains why the raw baseline would overstate the benefit (15% × 5.2 = 0.78).
- **The 10% floor removed.** The plausible range is now "no effect to about 20%" and is labelled as judgement. The report now says the downward bias from regression to the mean is unbounded by these data and could outweigh the traffic correction, so the 15% estimate is more likely too high than too low. Sensitivity analysis in Recommendation 6 now covers 0–20%, including 0–5%.
- **Speed claims softened.**
  - The bypass is now acknowledged as a possible cause of lower mean speeds, through removal of faster through-traffic.
  - The power-model figure is now a 13–17% range (powers of 1.5–2), and the summary and body match.
  - Agreement with the collision estimate is described as "not inconsistent". The claim that regression to the mean "may be modest" has been removed.
- **Diverted traffic addressed.** The report now asks whether the bypass is in the comparison group and which way that would bias the result. It also notes that drivers avoiding the cameras would move collisions elsewhere rather than prevent them. New Recommendation 3 covers both.
- **Interval caveat extended.** Overdispersion is now given as a second reason the −34% to +10% interval is too narrow.
- **Smaller points.**
  - The COVID caveat now notes that the direction of the bias is ambiguous and may partly offset regression to the mean.
  - The ~25% traffic fall at the 6 sites is now stated as conditional on the other 4 being unchanged.
  - The 4-vs-6 comparison carries a warning about noise (~20 collisions a year).
  - The longer baseline has moved to Recommendation 1.
- **Conclusions unchanged.** The central estimate stays at about 15%, a zero effect is still not excluded, and the advice against a city-wide programme stands. The stated uncertainty is wider, which strengthens that advice.
